stem.text: Let f be a twice-differentiable function with \( f(1) = -6 \) and \( f'(x) = 6 - 3 x^{2} \) for all x. Use the line tangent to the graph of f at x = 1 to approximate \( f(1.1) \). Is this approximation an overestimate or an underestimate of \( f(1.1) \)? Give a reason for the answer.

answer_key.label: The approximation is \( -5.7 \), and it is an overestimate, because \( f''(x) = - 6 x \) is negative for x > 0, so the graph of f is concave down and lies below its tangent line there.

worked_solution.text: The slope of the tangent line is \( f'(1) = 3 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: slope of the tangent line from the derivative

worked_solution.text: The tangent line at x = 1 is \( y = -6 + 3(x - 1) \).

worked_solution.rule_named: evaluate the tangent line at the nearby input

worked_solution.text: \( f''(x) = - 6 x \), which is negative for every x between 1 and 1.1. The graph is concave down there, so it lies below the tangent line and the approximation is an overestimate.
worked_solution.rule_named: concavity decides the direction of the error

options.label: The approximation is \( -5.7 \), and it is an underestimate, because \( f'(1) = 3 \) is positive, so f is increasing and its values rise above the starting value f(1).
options.derivation: the verdict decided from the sign of the first derivative, not from concavity
